name: Bee Gees
hook: Three brothers who began by sounding so like the Beatles that radio played them as the Beatles, then moved to Miami, found a falsetto, and built the biggest disco record of all on a two-bar tape loop.

blurb.age13: The Bee Gees were three brothers, Barry, Robin and Maurice Gibb. They were born on the Isle of Man, grew up partly in Manchester, and started the group in Australia in 1958. Their first big international hit, in 1967, sounded so much like the Beatles that American DJs played it thinking it was a secret Beatles record. In 1975, recording in Miami with the producer Arif Mardin, Barry started singing in a high falsetto and the band moved towards dance music. Their songs for the film 'Saturday Night Fever' (1977) made the soundtrack the best-selling album in history at the time. When their drummer had to leave in the middle of recording 'Stayin' Alive', they took two bars of drumming from another of their songs and looped them on tape. In 1979 a backlash against disco hit them hard in America.
blurb.adult: Formed in 1958 by Barry, Robin and Maurice Gibb, born on the Isle of Man to English parents, raised partly in Chorlton, Manchester, and from 1958 in Redcliffe, Queensland. Robert Stigwood managed their international career. 'New York Mining Disaster 1941' (April 1967) was sent to US radio in a blank sleeve with a hint that it was by an English group whose name began with B, and DJs played it as a Beatles record; Maurice Gibb later called it a rip-off of the Beatles, and George Harrison told him he had bought it because it sounded like them. Arif Mardin's 1975 sessions at Criteria in Miami for 'Main Course' moved them to R&B and gave Barry the falsetto that defined the rest of their career. The 'Saturday Night Fever' soundtrack (1977) became the best-selling album up to that time. 'Stayin'' Alive' was made after the drummer Dennis Bryon left the sessions when his mother died: the group and producer Albhy Galuten tried a drum machine, did not like it, and instead took two bars of the drums from 'Night Fever' and recorded them as a loop, crediting the drummer as 'Bernard Lupe' as a joke. It was a hand-made drum loop on one of the best-selling singles of the decade, years before samplers made that routine. The 1979 disco backlash, including Disco Demolition Night and radio stations' 'Bee Gee-free weekends', ended their run in America. Maurice died in 2003 and Robin in 2012.
